lessons.title: Fundamentals of Speed, Time and Distance
lessons.description: Understand the basic formulas, unit conversions and relationships between speed, time and distance.
lessons.content:
Speed, time and distance are fundamental quantitative aptitude concepts frequently tested in placement examinations.

Speed = Distance / Time
Distance = Speed × Time
Time = Distance / Speed

Units must be consistent before applying these formulas.

To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18.
To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5.

Example 1: A car travels 180 km in 3 hours. Speed = 180/3 = 60 km/h.

Example 2: A cyclist travels at 12 m/s for 50 seconds. Distance = 12 × 50 = 600 metres.

Example 3: A bus travels at 72 km/h. Its speed in m/s is 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.

Important concepts:
1. Constant speed means equal distances are covered in equal time intervals.
2. Average speed is total distance divided by total time.
3. If distance remains constant, speed and time are inversely proportional.
4. If time remains constant, speed and distance are directly proportional.

Placement tip: Always check whether the question uses kilometres, metres, hours, minutes or seconds before calculating.

lessons.title: Average Speed and Relative Speed
lessons.description: Calculate average speed and relative speed for objects moving in the same or opposite directions.
lessons.content:
Average speed measures total distance travelled per unit of total time.

Average Speed = Total Distance / Total Time.

Example: A person travels 60 km at 30 km/h and another 60 km at 60 km/h.
Time for first journey = 60/30 = 2 hours.
Time for second journey = 60/60 = 1 hour.
Total distance = 120 km.
Total time = 3 hours.
Average speed = 120/3 = 40 km/h.

For two equal-distance journeys at speeds a and b, average speed = 2ab/(a+b).

Relative speed describes how quickly the distance between two moving objects changes.

For two objects moving in opposite directions, relative speed = a+b.
For two objects moving in the same direction, relative speed = |a-b|.

Example: Two cars move towards each other at 40 km/h and 60 km/h. Their closing speed is 100 km/h.

If they are initially 200 km apart, meeting time = 200/100 = 2 hours.

Example: A faster car travels at 80 km/h and follows another travelling at 60 km/h. Their relative speed is 20 km/h. If the faster car is 40 km behind, catching time = 40/20 = 2 hours.

Important: The arithmetic mean of two speeds is not generally the average speed for equal-distance trips.

Placement tip: Draw arrows to represent travel directions before choosing whether to add or subtract speeds.

lessons.title: Problems on Trains
lessons.description: Solve train problems involving poles, platforms and trains moving in different directions.
lessons.content:
Train problems combine distance, speed and relative motion.

When a train crosses a pole or stationary person, the distance travelled is the train's length.

Time = Train Length / Train Speed.

Example: A 150-metre train moves at 54 km/h.
Speed = 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s.
Time to cross a pole = 150/15 = 10 seconds.

When a train crosses a platform, the total distance travelled is train length plus platform length.

Example: A 200-metre train crosses a 300-metre platform at 25 m/s.
Distance = 200+300 = 500 metres.
Time = 500/25 = 20 seconds.

When two trains cross each other, the distance is the sum of their lengths.

For trains travelling in opposite directions, add their speeds.
For trains travelling in the same direction, subtract the slower speed from the faster speed.

Example: Two trains of lengths 100 metres and 150 metres travel in opposite directions at 36 km/h and 54 km/h.
Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s.
Combined length = 250 metres.
Crossing time = 250/25 = 10 seconds.

Placement tip: Determine exactly what is being crossed before calculating the required distance.

lessons.title: Boats and Streams
lessons.description: Understand upstream speed, downstream speed and river-current problems.
lessons.content:
Boat and stream questions involve the speed of a boat in still water and the speed of the water current.

Let B = speed of boat in still water.
Let S = speed of stream.

Downstream speed = B+S.
Upstream speed = B-S, assuming B>S.

Boat speed in still water = (Downstream Speed + Upstream Speed)/2.
Stream speed = (Downstream Speed - Upstream Speed)/2.

Example: A boat moves downstream at 18 km/h and upstream at 12 km/h.
Boat speed = (18+12)/2 = 15 km/h.
Stream speed = (18-12)/2 = 3 km/h.

Example: A boat travels 24 km downstream at 12 km/h.
Time = 24/12 = 2 hours.

If its upstream speed is 8 km/h, the return journey takes 24/8 = 3 hours.

Total travel time = 5 hours.
Total distance = 48 km.
Average speed = 48/5 = 9.6 km/h.

Remember that the stream helps downstream movement and opposes upstream movement.

Placement tip: Write separate equations for upstream and downstream travel before solving.

lessons.title: Advanced Time Speed and Distance Problems
lessons.description: Apply relative motion, circular tracks, percentage changes and meeting-point strategies.
lessons.content:
Advanced speed and distance problems often combine several concepts.

Percentage changes in speed:
For a fixed distance, time is inversely proportional to speed.

If speed increases by 25%, the new time is original time divided by 1.25, representing a 20% decrease.

Example: A journey normally takes 5 hours. If speed increases by 25%, new time = 5/1.25 = 4 hours.

Circular tracks:
When two runners start together and move in opposite directions on a circular track, their first meeting time is track circumference divided by the sum of their speeds.

When they run in the same direction at different speeds, their first overtaking time is track circumference divided by the difference in their speeds.

Example: Two runners move in opposite directions at 4 m/s and 6 m/s on a 400-metre circular track.
Meeting time = 400/(4+6) = 40 seconds.

Meeting problems:
Two vehicles 300 km apart move towards each other at 70 km/h and 80 km/h.
Relative speed = 150 km/h.
Meeting time = 300/150 = 2 hours.

Delayed starts:
If a faster vehicle starts later, first calculate the distance already travelled by the slower vehicle. Then use relative speed to determine catching time.

Problem-solving strategy:
1. Identify the moving objects.
2. Convert units consistently.
3. Draw directions or a timeline.
4. Calculate relative speed if necessary.
5. Apply distance = speed × time.
6. Check whether the final result is reasonable.

Placement tip: Practice problems under timed conditions after mastering the underlying formulas.

exercises.title: Calculate Speed and Convert Units
exercises.description: Find the speed of a vehicle and convert it from km/h to m/s.
exercises.instructions: A bus travels 240 km in 4 hours. Calculate its speed in km/h and convert the result into m/s. Show all calculation steps.

exercises.title: Average Speed for Equal Distances
exercises.description: Calculate average speed when a vehicle travels equal distances at different speeds.
exercises.instructions: A car travels 90 km at 45 km/h and returns along the same route at 30 km/h. Calculate the total travel time and average speed.

exercises.title: Train Crossing a Platform
exercises.description: Solve a train problem involving train length and platform length.
exercises.instructions: A train 180 metres long moves at 54 km/h and crosses a platform 270 metres long. Calculate the time required to cross the platform completely.

exercises.title: Boat and Stream Calculation
exercises.description: Calculate the speed of a boat and the speed of a river current.
exercises.instructions: A boat travels downstream at 20 km/h and upstream at 12 km/h. Find the boat's speed in still water, the stream speed and the time required to travel 48 km upstream.

exercises.title: Relative Speed and Meeting Time Challenge
exercises.description: Solve a multi-step problem involving two vehicles travelling towards each other.
exercises.instructions: Two cities are 420 km apart. A car leaves the first city at 60 km/h. Another car leaves the second city 1 hour later at 80 km/h, travelling towards the first car. Calculate how long after the second car starts they meet and how far from the first city the meeting occurs.
